newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr retreats from highs but still strong in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dlr retreats from highs but still strong in Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar remained strong against the yen in late Tokyo on Monday, although it had retreated from the day's high of 113.96 yen in the face of profit-taking and corrective sales, dealers said.
But few expected the decline to continue, as the down side grew solid near 113.60 yen on buying from interbank operators and importers, and the yen remained weak in cross trade.
Sterling, the mark, and the Australian dollar were all big beneficiaries of the yen's weakness, with the pound rising briefly above 183 yen, its highest since January 1993, before falling back again.

"Fundamentally, the crosses are leading the market, where the yen is definitely no good right now. There's some talk that European funds may be selling yen and Japanese stocks to switch to well-performing European currencies and stocks," said a U.S. bank dealer in Tokyo.
A local bank dealer said the mark was heading for a test of the 75 yen level. It stood at 74.66/68 yen in late Tokyo.

Traders said the perception that Japan would not raise interest rates for the time being was making investment in Japanese assets less attractive, prompting investors to pour more cash into overseas assets with higher returns.

Although corrective selling had trimmed some of the dollar's gains by late afternoon, dealers said there were few signs of other substantial offers, and that the ease with which the greenback had broken through a psychologically important barrier of 113.60 yen suggested further rises were in store.
"There is no sense of completion," said one dealer, adding that the dollar was likely to hit 114 yen overseas today.

Active buying by interbank traders and investors in morning trade had quickly pushed the greenback through 113.60 yen, a level regarded as a strong psychological barrier because it was the highest since early January 1994, when then U.S. Treasury secretary Lloyd Bentsen voiced concern over depreciation of the yen.

The dollar then clung above this level for much of the morning, with a spatter of Australian dollar buying for yen nudging it higher in early afternoon, and a subsequent and more determined rush of yen sales in mid-afternoon pushing it to the day's high of 113.96 yen, the highest since April 1993.
Sterling hit a high of around 183.19 yen, while the Australian dollar posted a high of around 90.31 yen and the mark 74.81 yen.
A European bank dealer in Singapore said: "The Japanese economy is in a mess, the Nikkei doesn't look too great, interest rates are not going up -- they're just disinvesting."
He added that he saw the dollar going to 115 and then 117 yen, although he did not specify a time frame.
